title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a deepfake interview impersonating a public finance presenter and a government official endorsing an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The fake article was published online and designed to deceive investors into using a fraudulent trading service. The deployment failure was the absence of any verification that the interview occurred or that the officials had consented to be represented this way.

This shows a misuse of generative AI technology outside any legitimate deployment context. The system was not built to commit fraud, but it was used by scammers as a tool to fabricate credible-looking media content at scale. Catching this would have required readers to verify the interview through the officials directly or through the media outlet's own records, steps that many targets of investment scams do not take.

It is not established whether a single AI system generated all instances of this fraud or whether multiple systems were involved. The broader pattern shows scammers using AI-generated deepfakes as part of elaborate schemes that also include fake websites and false reviews.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featured a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article, which has since been removed, depicted Bullock storming out over Kohler's questions about the platform. This incident represents a growing category of scams that use artificial intelligence to create deepfake content featuring celebrities and politicians to promote fraudulent investments.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission data reveals these scams are becoming increasingly common and sophisticated. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams total, up 182 percent, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, businessman Dick Smith, and mining magnate Gina Rinehart are among the most frequently impersonated figures. Scammers build elaborate webs of fake websites, articles, and reviews to deceive investors. ASIC urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing.
